The two eliminated candidates who finished third and fourth in Laredo’s mayoral race say they have not endorsed anyone in the December 12 runoff — but both say the phone calls asking for their support started almost immediately, according to KGNS.

J.D. Gonzalez and Poncho Casso spoke with KGNS on its “Beyond the Headlines” panel, published November 8. In the first round, District 8 Councilwoman Alyssa Cigarroa finished first with just under 20,000 votes, about 35 percent, and incumbent Mayor Victor Treviño finished second with just under 18,000 votes, about 32 percent. Gonzalez finished third with just over 10,000 votes, Casso fourth with 10 percent, and Jorge Garza fifth with 1,600 votes.

Gonzalez, who described himself as the race’s “political rookie,” said getting more than 10,000 votes left him honored and humbled. He said his platform covered five areas — water, infrastructure, health care, business and economic development, and quality of life — along with promoting international trade and the USMCA and carrying a cohesive community message to state and federal leaders. He said he campaigned with integrity and would take an objective, positive approach focused on benefiting the majority rather than a select group.

His surprise of the campaign, he said, was how many voters told him elected officials reach out to everyone before taking office and then go “radio silence” once in office. He also said he appreciated being welcomed into people’s homes on the west and south sides of the city.

On endorsements, Gonzalez said he has received a lot of calls since the first day after the election but wants to stay neutral and open for now, because endorsing one side could mean losing “half your base.” He said his voters are intelligent and will vote for the better candidate, and that he would support whoever is willing to work on his platform — and if he does endorse, he will explain why. He named neither Cigarroa nor Treviño.

Casso, who called himself a “truth serum,” said his message was that incumbents are “making us poor as a community” through incompetence, corruption and greed, and that he offered to “take your tax away” and end what he called double taxation downtown. He said he ran in part because of the “brain drain” of talent leaving Laredo for lack of job opportunities, and he described his campaign as moving “towards hope.” He also argued the race was really about a proposed hospital, which he called a “cash cow,” and who would build it and hold the naming rights.

Unlike Gonzalez, Casso said he was not surprised by the result, saying he knew the outcome would be as it came out because, in his view, whoever spends the most money comes out on top. His one glimmer of hope, he said, was that the incumbents might be “blown out” and the runoff would be him and Gonzalez. He also recounted an election-day conversation with a former building-department head who told him permit turnaround had gone from 40 days to seven months and kept him talking for almost 30 minutes.

On endorsements, Casso said he has not backed anyone by name, though “the emissaries are coming like I’ve never seen before” seeking his support. He said the only reason he would endorse someone is if he thinks that person can be coached “to do the right thing,” and that if he does endorse, he would have to explain why “Choice B is better” for Laredo — but he did not say who “Choice B” is.

Both men left their own political futures open. Gonzalez said “there’ll be more JD to come,” and Casso called it “a chess game,” adding, “I don’t want to give it out right now.”

Source: KGNS, November 8, 2026.

title: Eliminated mayoral hopefuls Casso and Gonzalez stay neutral — for now — as runoff endorsement calls pour in
